--- title: 'PE100-02: Types, Variables, and Operators' --- Niklaus Wirth was one of the founding giants of Computer Science. He wrote an introductory textbook whose title neatly summed up the act and art of programming: [Algorithms + Data Structures = Programs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algorithms_%2B_Data_Structures_%3D_Programs). Data Structures are how information is stored in a computer, and algorithms are the instructions the computer applies to transform that data. To run the code in a cell, first click in the cell to select it. Then you can **either**: 1. Go to the "Run" menu and choose "Run Selected Cells", or 1. Just press Shift + Enter. Let's do this now: click just below where it says "print (403.616"), then Go to the "Run" menu and choose "Run Selected Cells". ::: {#e16d42ed-aee8-409f-a5ed-2bd58a262890 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} print (403.616) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` 403.616 ``` ::: ::: When it ran, it printed "403.616" on a line by itself. That was the output from the print. Click in the next cell (where it says "103.5") to select that cell. Then hold down the Shift key while you press Enter. ::: {#7d1fb3e9-c37d-4867-ac04-1b1a4f907cff .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} 103.5 ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` 103.5 ``` ::: ::: In Python, and in Jupyter notebooks, if the last (or only!) line evaluates to some value then it will be printed out. That's how "103.5" got printed - a literal number evaluates to that number when it's run. A "literal number" means you look at it in your code and you _literally see a number_. Take a look at a _string literal_. Run each of the next two cells... ::: {#ce6d68bb-7c98-4dcf-894e-e519dc7fb367 .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} print ("the quick brown fox") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` the quick brown fox ``` ::: ::: ::: {#b907d685-1c2b-4dc4-a627-bf8c98f2b872 .cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code} print ('jumped over the lazy dogs') ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` jumped over the lazy dogs ``` ::: ::: At this point, we can use Python and Jupyter Lab as a scientific calculator. We have some literals of different types (int, real, and string, so far) and we can print them out with the ```print()``` *function*. If we don't explicitly print anything at the end of a cell, Python will show us the last value that was computed. ## Operators Like any programming language, Python lets you "do math" and lots of other things. Let's take a look at some of the basic "operators". In all of the code-containing cells through this course, try to predict what will happen first, and then run the code. ::: {#99b2c0e4-14aa-466a-8a25-f22604271bb8 .cell execution_count=5} ``` {.python .cell-code} 2+2 ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=5} ``` 4 ``` ::: ::: ::: {#90383055-7b1b-47ca-8e6b-38fef949ee8f .cell execution_count=6} ``` {.python .cell-code} 2*8 ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=6} ``` 16 ``` ::: ::: ::: {#5c7336fe-ebd6-4596-8dd3-7d85e24c729d .cell execution_count=7} ``` {.python .cell-code} 6-4 ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=7} ``` 2 ``` ::: ::: ::: {#ffe5e208-cd79-46ba-9985-68f2b414aa5d .cell execution_count=8} ``` {.python .cell-code} 7*6 ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=8} ``` 42 ``` ::: ::: ::: {#28754cd0-96b2-4e55-9cc7-b3eb978c2f93 .cell execution_count=9} ``` {.python .cell-code} 16/3 ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=9} ``` 5.333333333333333 ``` ::: ::: Besides the "classic" operators, there are some handy extras: ::: {#59753692-d36a-40d7-858b-04fcd629b4c1 .cell execution_count=10} ``` {.python .cell-code} 16//3 ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=10} ``` 5 ``` ::: ::: What happened there? The ```//``` operator does *integer division* - it returns the whole number part of the answer, just like when we learned division in elementary school. ::: {#dac9ed9b-95d6-41b3-ab3b-0b1229d8ef15 .cell execution_count=11} ``` {.python .cell-code} 16%3 ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=11} ``` 1 ``` ::: ::: The ```%``` operator returns the remainder. This is also called "modulo", and the above would be pronounced "sixteen mod 3". ::: {#1177f56b-554c-4c41-b85a-af6a2bc73a6a .cell execution_count=12} ``` {.python .cell-code} 2**8 ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=12} ``` 256 ``` ::: ::: ::: {#0b991148-b2ad-4f90-866a-ff1c7a227007 .cell execution_count=13} ``` {.python .cell-code} 4**2.718281828459045 ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=13} ``` 43.30806042677592 ``` ::: ::: The ```**``` operator does exponentiation. The *arguments* can be integers or they can be real numbers. Naturally, operators can be combined into arbitrarily long *expressions*. ::: {#f625e6fc-3ca6-47b7-ba35-76c420da2317 .cell execution_count=14} ``` {.python .cell-code} 3*4*5 ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=14} ``` 60 ``` ::: ::: ::: {#49d8fdb7-7d0c-43bb-9db8-b4dd3700fc5e .cell execution_count=15} ``` {.python .cell-code} 6+4*5 ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=15} ``` 26 ``` ::: ::: Notice what happens when we use different operators. They are applied in the "My Dear Aunt Sally" order of precendence (multiplication, division, addition, subtraction). Order of operations: Exponentiation: ```**```\ Multiplication, Division, Remainder: ```* / // %```\ Addition and Subtraction: ```+ -``` Within the same level, operators are applied left-to-right. 8-5+2 is evaluated as 3+2 and yields 5. The exception is exponentiation: 2 ** 3 ** 4 is treated as 2 ** 81 and yeilds an annoyingly large number ::: {#3f0ff4ca-da1e-4097-873e-cb61bbd7a22f .cell execution_count=16} ``` {.python .cell-code} print (2**3**4) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` 2417851639229258349412352 ``` ::: ::: ::: {#4aebc6f8-d3c5-422e-8d31-6664552ad4ce .cell execution_count=17} ``` {.python .cell-code} print (2**81) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` 2417851639229258349412352 ``` ::: ::: ## Variables Unless we just use Jupyter as a big, expensive scientific calculator, we need a way to store data. *Variables* were invented for just that purpose, and virtually every language has them. Think of them as a place to store data of some kind, and that place has a name. They behave in Python just like you'd expect. ::: {#6350b83c-2d85-4cc2-a54c-d8bf18c6d42c .cell execution_count=18} ``` {.python .cell-code} answer = 42 print(answer) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` 42 ``` ::: ::: We just created a variable named ```answer``` and gave it the value 42. Variables are long-lived - later we'll talk about just how long when we start writing our own functions, but until then our variables last as long as Python (or in our case, Jupyter) is running. Take a look - answer is still there. ::: {#56538fe2-b464-4fe1-a3e0-23ff1b555bda .cell execution_count=19} ``` {.python .cell-code} print(answer) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` 42 ``` ::: ::: The value stored in a variable can change. It can even change type: ::: {#58211df3-28e4-4829-b5ca-ab9174213bcd .cell execution_count=20} ``` {.python .cell-code} weight = 60 weight = 70 print(weight) weight = "not very much." print(weight) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` 70 not very much. ``` ::: ::: We can declare many variables, and we can "do things" with them just like we can when we type in numbers or strings. ::: {#74124737-2572-46e4-a696-a91f35cea69b .cell execution_count=21} ``` {.python .cell-code} volts = 120 amps = 4 watts = volts * amps watts ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=21} ``` 480 ``` ::: ::: In the last line, we just put ```watts``` because Jupyter automatically prints what the last line evaluates to. We can use variables to change the *order of operations*. Let's see the average price of two people's meals: ::: {#1600a8b8-7222-4bf7-8f63-4fce4b3bd56d .cell execution_count=22} ``` {.python .cell-code} total = 22.41 + 19.45 average = total / 2 average ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=22} ``` 20.93 ``` ::: ::: That's the right answer. If we hadn't done that, we would have gotten ::: {#199989df-a1c7-41fd-8088-19107e5025c3 .cell execution_count=23} ``` {.python .cell-code} 22.41 + 19.45 / 2 ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=23} ``` 32.135 ``` ::: ::: which is utterly wrong. Beware of the order of operations... it is a frequent source of bugs in scientific programming. #### Variable Naming Rules For the most part, you can pick whatever name makes sense for a variable, but there *are* some rules. When choosing a name: 1. No keywords (```False``` won't work.) 1. No spaces (```sample thickness``` is invalid) 1. The first character **must** be one of * a-z, or A-Z, or _. (the underscore character) * As a result, no numbers (3rd_sample_holder is invalid) 1. **After** the first character, you can then have numbers (sample_holder_3 is perfectly valid) 1. No other symbols are allowed (exploded&destroyed_spectrometers is invalid, and probably suggests it's time to review lab safety procedures). **Note: Uppercase vs. Lowercase matters!** ```Bevatron``` is not the same variable as ```bevatron``` ## Types We've hinted that variables have a "type", and that the type can change if it needs to. The way it works is that variables keep track of what *type* they are (integer, real number, or string) and what their "value" is. We can even interrogate a variable as see what type it is: ::: {#fc59a93c-4ce8-4f62-a804-34d8ea496926 .cell execution_count=24} ``` {.python .cell-code} reading=7.2 print("reading:") print(type(reading)) reading="rainbow" # changes type of reading to string print(type(reading)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` reading: ``` ::: ::: ::: {#2fc7b814-7512-4fb5-b81b-b103599d0cba .cell execution_count=25} ``` {.python .cell-code} my_number = 42 my_string = "was that really the right answer?" first_type = type(my_number) second_type = type(my_string) print(first_type, second_type) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` ``` ::: ::: The type of a variable matters. Let's create a variable with an integer in it and another with a string. Then let's do some math: ::: {#209a9284-072b-41e2-82aa-1ef4b62d39fa .cell execution_count=26} ``` {.python .cell-code} first_thing = 6 second_thing = 7 print (first_thing + second_thing) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` 13 ``` ::: ::: On the other hand, if we tried to do the following: first_thing = 6\ second_thing = "7"\ print (first_thing + second_thing) Then we would get an error message. Go ahead and try it - put quotation marks around the code cell we ran before and execute it. How do we handle situations like that, where `second_thing` held a string representing a seven, but because it was a string variable it couldn't be used as an integer? Python provides a few functions to convert values from one type to another. The `str()` function takes a variable and converts it to a string. The `float()` and `int()` functions convert their arguments to floating-point and to integer numbers, respectively. ::: {#8b0fa20d-3cf4-4e9d-9c66-28619c8598b6 .cell execution_count=27} ``` {.python .cell-code} print(first_thing + int(second_thing)) print(first_thing + float(second_thing)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` 13 13.0 ``` ::: ::: Being able to convert values from one type to another is often called *type coercion*. These conversions are extremely important for situation where you need to get input from a user, even more so if you need to do it repetitively. ## Continuation Character Sometimes the expressions we need to evaluate can be very long. It would be nice if we could split up a long expression and spread it out over a few lines. As a small example, we'll take a look at 4+2+3. Many programming languages will let us split an expression anywhere we want, such as: ::: {#c4e88656-191d-479f-9dcf-d5c8020a1cce .cell execution_count=28} ``` {.python .cell-code} 4+2 +3 ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=28} ``` 3 ``` ::: ::: ...but that result isn't right in Python. The last line, `+3`, was evaluated and printed as the result of running that cell. In Python,it turns out, if we need to continue an expression on the next line we must end the current line with a backslash `\` and press enter. It has to be a backslash, by the way, and **cannot** be the forward slash like we use for division. ::: {#a3f81522-1f91-4fc5-92d8-02d8d88d208f .cell execution_count=29} ``` {.python .cell-code} 4+2\ +3 ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=29} ``` 9 ``` ::: ::: Time for an exercise! Predict what will be printed when you run the next cell. Then, run the next cell and see how you did. If you miss one, make sure you figure out what happened before you go. I know, we're professionals, I shouldn't have to say that... ::: {#a7509f39-e1b5-4581-9294-6837652e2448 .cell execution_count=30} ``` {.python .cell-code} print(1 + 3 + 5 * 4 / 2) print(7 % 2 * 10) big_num = 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 \ + 5 + 6 print(big_num) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` 14.0 10 21 ``` ::: ::: Now write an expression to average three numbers (12, 14, and 66), divide the result by three, and square it. You can use the code cell right below here, if you're working along inside the notebook: ## The String Type At the beginning of this notebook, we casually mentioned "strings" without saying what they are. They're just "sequences of characters". And these can be any kind of characters - the English alphabet, the Hungarian alphabet, hiragana... it doesn't matter. ::: {#2db2513c-9836-444f-bb61-0a8e65d12eac .cell execution_count=32} ``` {.python .cell-code} print("I'll see you mañana, assuming I don't get irradiated to death.") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` I'll see you mañana, assuming I don't get irradiated to death. ``` ::: ::: Some, probably most, programming languages contain strings inside "double quotes", ```"```, which is shift+apostrophe on US English keyboards. Other languages (SQL and Pascal are the only two I can think of) use single quotes: ```'```. Python lets you use either one. You *do* have to be consistent in each string, but it can vary from one string to the next: ::: {#614bce71-4826-4646-80b5-c8681aec3581 .cell execution_count=33} ``` {.python .cell-code} print("double quotes work") print('single quotes also work') print('but do not mix the two in one string!" ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-error} ::: {.ansi-escaped-output} ```{=html} 
  Cell In[32], line 3
    print('but do not mix the two in one string!"
                                                 ^
SyntaxError: EOL while scanning string literal
``` ::: ::: ::: Because we can use either type of quotation mark, we can exploit that to let us put quotation marks into strings: ::: {#d7be27f7-1a62-4e9f-a488-99fd10f3e424 .cell execution_count=34} ``` {.python .cell-code} print("Don't put explosive mixtures in the spectrometer, please.") print('We warned him... "Do not turn the spectrometer into a bomb!" but he still did it.') ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Don't put explosive mixtures in the spectrometer, please. We warned him... "Do not turn the spectrometer into a bomb!" but he still did it. ``` ::: ::: That lets us embed whichever kind of quotation mark we need into a string. But what if we need to embed **both** kinds of quotes into one string? We're in luck: we can use the backslash character again to "quote" our quotation mark. In fact, we can quote any character with it if we need to. ::: {#2cd4377a-518b-4df0-87f2-bb4931185921 .cell execution_count=35} ``` {.python .cell-code} print("We told him \"Hexanitrohexaazaisowurtzitane and spectrometers don't mix\", but we're pretty sure he ignored us.") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` We told him "Hexanitrohexaazaisowurtzitane and spectrometers don't mix", but we're pretty sure he ignored us. ``` ::: ::: That sentence contains three things, all inside the string itself: 1. Double Quotes to surround a direct quotation 2. A single quote, also called an apostrophe depending on how it's used, to make a contraction, and 3. A totally awesome and terrifying molecule you have to google to believe. OK, I'll save you the trouble. [Prepare to lose most of a day's productivity](https://www.science.org/content/blog-post/things-i-won-t-work-hexanitrohexaazaisowurtzitane). You're welcome. (Derek has written gobs of articles on fun substances. [Here are some more.](https://www.science.org/topic/blog-category/things-i-wont-work-with) ) There is one last kind of string literal. Sometimes you need a string that is several lines long. The "triple quote" is a way to do it. You have to use three double-quotes in a row: ::: {#5a967aae-73d7-48b4-b6b9-91e9c8863b59 .cell execution_count=36} ``` {.python .cell-code} gigantic = """This is the first line, This is the second, and this is the third and final line of my string.""" print(gigantic) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` This is the first line, This is the second, and this is the third and final line of my string. ``` ::: ::: Triple quotes are also an easier way to embed mixed kinds of quotation marks into strings: ::: {#2652937d-4643-4c76-9f70-a364b9dc7cf2 .cell execution_count=37} ``` {.python .cell-code} movie_opinion = """I know people who say "The Avengers" isn’t a good movie, but I don’t agree.""" print(movie_opinion) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` I know people who say "The Avengers" isn’t a good movie, but I don’t agree. ``` ::: ::: ## Coming Up Next We just looked at enough of Python and Jupyter notebooks to use it as a basic calculator, but so far we can't do any real, general-purpose programming with it. The "flow of control" so far as been a straight line from top to bottom and we can't change what we're doing in response to different inputs. That's about to change. In the next section we'll look at the ```if``` statement and how to use it.
